en: The Daśapadārtha-śāstra (Treatise on the Ten Categories of the Victorious School), one fascicle.
Composed by the Victor Vidyākaraśānti;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
There are ten categories of meaning:
first, substance; second, quality; third, activity; fourth, generality; fifth, particularity; sixth, inherence; seventh, potency; eighth, non-potency; ninth, partiality; and tenth, the ineffable.
What is the meaning of the term "real category" (vastu-pada)?
It refers to nine kinds of realities which constitute the meaning of the real category. What are these nine?
One is earth, two is water, three is fire, four is wind, five is space, six is time, seven is direction, eight is the self, and nine is the mind.
These are the nine realities.
What is earth?
That which possesses visible form, taste, odor, and tangibility is earth.
What is water? That which possesses visible form, taste, and tangibility, as well as fluidity and moisture, is water.
What is fire? That which possesses visible form and tangibility is fire.
What is wind? It is said that only tangibility constitutes wind.
What is space? It is said that only sound constitutes space.
What is time? It is said that time is the causal condition for designating "this" and "that," "together" and "not together," "slow" and "fast."
What is meant by "direction"? That which serves as the referential cause for designating east, south, west, north, and so forth, is called direction.

What is meant by "self"? That which has the characteristic of cognition arising from the causal conditions of the conjunction of pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, effort, volition, dharma, and adharma, is called self.

What is the nature of the mind? It is characterized by the cognition that arises from the causal conditions of the non-conjunction of factors such as the perception of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, and the practice of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; this is the mind.
What is the category-meaning of "quality" (guṇa)?
The twenty-four qualities are termed the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*).

What are these twenty-four qualities? First, color; second, taste; third, odor; fourth, tangibility; fifth, number; sixth, dimension; seventh, distinctness; eighth, conjunction; ninth, disjunction; tenth, thatness; eleventh, thisness; twelfth, cognition; thirteenth, pleasure; fourteenth, pain; fifteenth, desire; sixteenth, aversion; seventeenth, effort; eighteenth, gravity; nineteenth, fluidity; twentieth, viscidity; twenty-first, motion; twenty-second, dharma; twenty-third, adharma; and twenty-fourth, sound.
These constitute the twenty-four qualities.
What is form (*rūpa*)? It refers to that which is apprehended solely by the eye, based on the single designation "form.
What is taste (*rasa*)? It refers to that which is apprehended solely by the tongue, based on the single designation "taste."
What is fragrance (*gandha*)? It refers to that which is apprehended solely by the nose; it is designated as "fragrance" based on its single substratum.
What is tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*)? It refers to that which is apprehended solely by the skin;

it is designated as "tangibility" based on its single substratum. What is number (*saṃkhyā*)? It refers to the cause for the conceptual cognition and verbal designation of "one," "non-one," "real," "composite," "unified," and so forth, regarding all real entities; it is the name "number" applied to such unities.
What is measure (*pramāṇa*)? It refers to minute bodies, large bodies, short bodies, long bodies, spherical bodies, and so forth; these are called measure.
Regarding "minute bodies":
This means that two subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) serve as the causal conditions for conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
and from the production of these two entities,
one real subtle atom is designated as the causal condition for cognition; this is called the substance of shortness (*hrasva*).
Regarding "longness as substance":
this refers to the aggregation of the results of three atoms (*paramāṇu*),
which are produced through the differentiation of accumulation based on a plurality of substances and longness as substance.
A single real entity that serves as the conditioning cause for a large [unit] is called a "large substance" (*mahā-dravya*).
As for a "short substance," it is produced by two substances acting as the combined causal conditions, namely, two atoms (*paramāṇu*) serving as the fruit;
a single real entity that serves as the conditioning cause for a short [unit] is called a "short substance."
Regarding the substance of length (*dīrghatva*): it refers to the substance of length arising from the accumulation of multiple substances.

It is the cause for the conceptual designation of "length" based on the synthesis of the three atoms (*paramāṇu*) and their effects, which are produced through specific aggregations; this is termed the substance of length.
Regarding the spherical entity,
there are two kinds: first,
the infinitesimal atom (paramāṇu), and second, the infinitely large.
An atom (*paramāṇu*) refers to that which is the basis for the designation and cognition of a single, real atom resulting from the aggregation of atoms; this is called an atom.
As for the "extremely large" (*paramamahat*):

That is to say, space, time, direction, the self (ātman), substance (dravya), inherence (samavāya), the single reality (ekattva), the ultimate (paramārtha), the great (mahat), the designator (abhidhāna), the object of cognition (ālambana), the cause (hetu), and that which is also called "pervasive" (sarvatraga)—these are termed "the Great.
What is their distinct nature?

That is to say, when all real entities are combined into one, yet are not a single real entity, and serve as the causal conditions for distinct designations such as "one" or "distinct substance," this is called "distinct substance.
What is "conjunction"?
It is said that when two things that were previously non-attaining reach a state of attaining, it is called conjunction.
This is of three kinds: first, arising from a single karma; second, arising from both karmas;
and third, arising from their combination.
Arising from a single karma refers to that which arises from movement or from non-movement.
"Born from both types of karma" means that it arises from two kinds of movement.
"Born from conjunction" means...
This means that when many substances arise without movement, they coincide with space;
how then can one speak of "separation"? Separation is defined as the state from the second [moment] onward until non-arrival.
This has three types: first, arising from a single action; second, arising from both actions; and third, arising from separation.
Among these, the production through individual karma and the production through simultaneous karma are explained together as previously stated.

"Production through separation" refers to when a fruit that has already been produced is separated from its remaining causes; it is like the destruction of the fruit or its becoming empty through such separation.

What is its essence? It refers to that which is produced by a single reality, which is depended upon by a cognition of "one" regarding things such as those occurring at the same time; it is the causal basis for the conceptualization and verbal expression of that [reality], and this is called its essence.

What is this essence? It refers to that which is produced by a single reality, which is depended upon by a cognition of "one" regarding things such as those occurring at the same time, when [the objects] are proximate.
This refers to the cause of cognition, which is designated as its substance (*tattva*).
What is awakening? It is the realization of all objects.
This is of two kinds: first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); second, inference (*anumāna*).

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the arising of a cognition that has the aspect of an object when there is a conjunction of the sense faculties and so forth with real entities such as visible form; this is called direct perception.
Inference (*anumāna*) is of two kinds.

Inference based on seeing similarity is so called because one sees the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and, through the recollection of the connection between the characteristic and the characterized (*lakṣya*), the mind and the object are conjoined.

Inference based on not seeing similarity is so called because [the object] is not seen. Inference based on seeing similarity refers to the conjunction of the self and the mind, due to the recollection of the relationship between the characteristic and the characterized upon seeing the characteristic.
When knowledge arises regarding an unperceived object of characterization (*lakṣya*), it is called "inference by similarity" (*sādharmya-anumāna*).

Regarding "inference by dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya-anumāna*): it refers to [inferring] because one perceives the connection between cause and effect, the unity of a single referent, or a contradiction; because one relies on the recollection of that connection; and because of the conjunction of the self and the mind.
The cognition that arises regarding an object that is ultimately not perceived is called "inference by similarity" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
What is pleasure? It is defined as the nature of satisfaction belonging to the qualities of a single, substantial self.
What is suffering (*duḥkha*)? It refers to the essential nature of a single, real self that is afflicted by its own qualities;
this is called suffering. What is desire (*chanda*)? It refers to the longing for the union of a single, real self with form and other objects; this is called desire.
What is hatred (*dveṣa*)? It refers to the harm caused toward form and other objects by a single, substantial self;

this is called hatred. What is effort (*vīrya*)? It refers to the exertion produced by the conjunction of a single, substantial self with desire, hatred, and the mental faculty; this is called effort.

What is the nature of heaviness? It refers to the actual combination of earth and water, wherein one constituent element is the cause for falling downward; this is called the nature of heaviness. What is the nature of fluidity?
It refers to the actual combination of earth, water, and fire, wherein one constituent element is the cause for flowing; this is called the nature of fluidity.
What is moisture? It refers to the water-element being conjoined with a single substance; the cause that gathers earth and so forth is called moisture.
What is action? This is of two kinds: first, the cause as thought (cetanā), and second, the cause as formation (abhisamskāra).

The cause of recollection (*smṛti-hetu*) refers to the specific cultivation produced by the practice of inferential cognition (*anumāna-pratyakṣa*) through the realization of the unity of the self; this is called the cause of recollection.

The cause of action (*kriyā-hetu*) refers to the functional capacity (*śakti*) inherent in a single, substantially existent, and resistant entity, which is produced by actions such as throwing or tossing; this is called the cause of action.
"Activity" refers to functional efficacy.
Regarding phenomena (*dharma*), there are two types: first, that which can turn [toward], and second, that which can return.

That which can turn refers to the fact that the agreeable body and so forth—which are causes of pleasure—are in union with a self (*ātman*) as a single, real entity, yet this is contrary to the production of their fruit; this is called "that which can turn."

That which is capable of returning refers to that which is contrary to the fruit—namely, detachment from defilements, objective conditions, correct wisdom, joy, the cause of self, and the unity of the real—which is called "capable of returning.
What is non-dharma? It refers to the causes of unpleasantness, such as bodily suffering, and false wisdom.
That which is unified with [the cause] yet contradicts the nature of the fruit is called "unrighteous" (*adharma*).
What is sound? It refers to that which is apprehended solely by the ear and rests upon a single basis;
this is called sound. What is the category of action (*karmapada*)? It refers to the five kinds of action; these are called the category of action.

What are these five? First, the action of grasping; second, the action of relinquishing; third, the action of contraction; fourth, the action of extension; and fifth, the action of motion. What is the action of grasping?

It refers to the cause for the conjunction or disjunction of atoms and so forth in locations such as the upper, lower, or cardinal directions, or in space; based upon this single reality, it is called the action of grasping.

What is the action of relinquishing (*visarpaṇa-karman*)? It refers to the cause for the conjunction and disjunction of atoms and so forth in locations such as the upper, lower, and intermediate directions, or in space;

that which depends on a single real entity is called the action of relinquishing. What is the action of contraction (*ākuñcana-karman*)? It refers to the cause for the conjunction of a large, long real entity with a proximate location and the disjunction from a remote location while depending on a single real entity; this is called the action of contraction.

What is the action of extension (*prasāraṇa-karman*)? It refers to that which, in dependence upon a single substantial entity (*dravya*) located in proximity to a large, long, and solid [object], possesses the causes for the separation from or conjunction with distant or proximate locations; this is called the action of extension. What is the action of contraction (*saṃkoca-karman*)?

It refers to all obstructive substantial entities in conjunction, which, in dependence upon a single substantial entity, possess the causes for conjunction or separation; this is called the action of contraction.
What is the meaning of the term "existent" (*sat*)?
What constitutes existence? It refers to that which is conjoined with all categories (*padārtha*)—substance, quality, and action—and is apprehended by all the sense faculties.
That which serves as the cause for the cognition that expresses [the categories of] substance, quality, and action is called "existence" (sattā).
What is the category of "distinctness" (anyatva)? It is that which is eternal, resides in substances, and depends upon a single substance;
it is named the category of distinctness because it is the cause for the cognition that excludes those [other things] and the cause for the cognition that expresses this [distinctness].

What is the meaning of the term "conjunction" (*samudāya*)? It refers to that which causes the real entities (*dravya*) and so forth not to be separated from one another, being mutually connected; it is the cause for the cognition that expresses [this].
Furthermore, the nature of being a single entity is the meaning of conjunction.
What is the meaning of "possessing capacity" (*samartha*)? It refers to the real entities, qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karma*) being conjoined together.
Alternatively, it may be that various [factors] produce their respective fruits according to what is strictly required.
This is called the meaning of the term "possibility" (*sāmarthya*).
What is the meaning of the term "impossibility" (*asāmarthya*)? It refers to the conjunction of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).
Alternatively, when a certain [cause] does not produce other effects but is strictly required for a specific one, this is termed the "meaning of incapacity" (*aśakti-pada*).

What is the "meaning of commonality" (*sāmānya-pada*)? It refers to substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), activity-ness (*karmatva*), their unity (*ekatva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), form-ness (*rūpatva*), and grasping-ness (*grahaṇatva*).
This is called the meaning of the term "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*).
As for "real nature" (*dravyatva*): it refers to the fact that all substances (*dravya*) are combined within all substances as the causal basis for the designation of "substance.
It does not apply to qualities (*guṇa*) or activities (*karman*), and that which is apprehended by visual contact is called real nature.
The nature of virtue (guṇatva) refers to the conjunction of all virtues within all virtues; it is the causal condition for the designation of "virtue.
That which does not deviate from its actual function and is apprehended by all faculties is called the nature of virtue.
The nature of action (*karmatva*) refers to all actions being conjoined with all actions as the causal basis for the designation of "action.
It does not apply to substance (*dravya*) or quality (*guṇa*); that which is apprehended by visual contact is called the nature of action.
The nature of the stages (*bhūmi*) is also like this.
Regarding the "inexpressible meaning" (*anabhilāpyārtha*), what is meant by the five kinds of nameless and inexpressible meanings? What are these five?

First, non-existence of the unarisen; second, non-existence of the ceased; third, mutual non-existence; fourth, non-existence of non-encounter; fifth, ultimate non-existence—these are called the five kinds of non-existence.

Regarding the non-existence of the unarisen: it refers to the fact that when substance, quality, and activity have not yet arisen because their causes and conditions have not come together, it is termed the non-existence of the unarisen.

"Non-existence through cessation" refers to when real entities—such as substances, qualities, or actions—cease due to the exhaustion of their causal momentum or the arising of contrary conditions; although they have arisen, they are destroyed and thus termed "non-existence through cessation.
"Mutual non-existence" refers to the mutual absence of various substances and so forth among one another, which is termed "mutual non-existence."

“Non-occurrence through non-union” refers to cases where there is no conjunction or combination with respect to a certain thing, such as its essential nature or reality; this is termed non-occurrence through non-union.
“Ultimate non-existence” refers to that which, due to the absence of causes, does not arise at any of the three times and never originates; this is termed ultimate non-existence.
Among these nine substances, how many possess motion and how many are devoid of motion?
Five possess motion—namely earth, water, fire, wind, and mind—while four are devoid of motion—namely the remaining [four] substances.
Just as with movement and non-movement, resistance and non-resistance,
possession of functional power and lack of functional power, and having a distinct individuality versus lacking a distinct individuality, it should be understood that the same applies here.
Among these nine realities, how many possess qualities (*guṇa*) and how many lack qualities?
All possess qualities; there is no reality that lacks qualities.
Just as all possess qualities, so too do they exist through the conjunction of causes and conditions, possessing both a real nature and distinctness.
The same applies to the non-contradiction with their effects and their dependence on causes.
Thus, among the nine substances, how many possess tangibility and how many lack it?
Four possess tangibility—namely, earth, water, fire, and wind; five lack tangibility—namely, the remaining substances.

The same applies to contact and non-contact, the primary elements (*bhūta*), the derived matter (*bhautika*), substance (*dravya*), reality (*satya*), qualities (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), causes (*hetu*), and common and uncommon [factors].
Among these nine realities, how many are with form (*rūpin*) and how many are without form (*arūpin*)?
Three are with form, namely earth, water, and fire; six are without form, namely the remaining realities.
As it is with the formless and the form realms, so it is with the visible and the invisible, and with the resistant and the non-resistant eye.
Thus, there are nine real entities and five constant categories.
That is to say, among these four, that which is not derived is permanent, while that which is derived is impermanent.
As with permanence and impermanence, so too are there the causes of being real or unreal, and having parts or being partless.
Non-contradiction, non-causality, non-contradiction, non-extremity, having difference, having difference, non-perfection, and perfection—likewise.
Thus, there are nine realities: five are faculties and four are non-faculties.
What are these five? They are earth, water, fire, wind, and space as the faculties.
Thus, among these five faculties, the nose faculty is earth; the tongue faculty is water; the eye faculty is fire; the body faculty is wind; and the ear faculty is space.
These nine real substances are said to possess qualities by virtue of how many qualities?

That is to say, by fourteen. What are these fourteen? First, color; second, taste; third, odor; fourth, tangibility; fifth, number; sixth, dimension; seventh, distinctness; eighth, conjunction; ninth, disjunction; tenth, that-ness; eleventh, this-ness; twelfth, weight; thirteenth, fluidity; and fourteenth, motion.
By how many qualities is water said to possess qualities?
It is by fourteen. What are these fourteen?

1. Color, 2. Taste, 3. Tangibility, 4. Number, 5. Dimension, 6. Distinctness of Substance, 7. Conjunction, 8. Disjunction, 9. That-ness (remoteness), 10. This-ness (proximity), 11. Weight, 12. Fluidity.
The thirteenth is moisture and the fourteenth is motion.
By how many qualities is fire said to possess qualities?
It is said to possess them by way of eleven.

What are the eleven? First, color; second, touch; third, number; fourth, dimension; fifth, distinctness; sixth, conjunction; seventh, disjunction; eighth, that-ness; ninth, this-ness; tenth, fluidity; eleventh, motion.
By how many qualities is wind said to possess qualities?
It is by nine. Which nine?
First, number; second, dimension; third, distinctness; fourth, conjunction; fifth, disjunction; sixth, that-ness; seventh, this-ness; eighth, tangibility; and ninth, motion.
By how many qualities is space said to possess qualities?
It is by six. What are these six?
First, number; second, dimension; third, distinctness; fourth, conjunction; fifth, disjunction; and sixth, sound.
At that time, by how many qualities is it said to possess qualities?
It is by five. What are these five?
First, number; second, magnitude; third, distinctness; fourth, conjunction; and fifth, disjunction.
As it is with time and direction, so it is with me.
By how many qualities am I said to possess qualities?
Namely, by fourteen.

What are these fourteen? First, number; second, magnitude; third, distinctness; fourth, conjunction; fifth, disjunction; sixth, cognition; seventh, pleasure; eighth, pain; ninth, desire; tenth, hatred; eleventh, effort; twelfth, dharma; thirteenth, adharma; and fourteenth, motion.
By how many qualities is the mind said to possess qualities?
It is by eight. What are these eight?
First, number; second, measure; third, distinctness; fourth, conjunction; fifth, disjunction; sixth, that-ness; seventh, this-ness; eighth, motion.
Among these twenty-four qualities, such as form and so forth, how many are present objects and how many are not present objects?
Form, taste, odor, and tangibility may be either present objects or not present objects.
What is a manifest object?
It refers to that which, depending upon the great [elements], is not a single reality; this is called a manifest object.
What is a non-manifest object?
That is to say, those things that depend upon atoms or the effects of two atoms are called non-manifest objects (*aparokṣa-viṣaya*).

Sound is entirely a manifest object, as are color, taste, fragrance, tangibility, number, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, "that-ness," "this-ness," fluidity, moisture, heaviness, and momentum; these are likewise [manifest objects].
Pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and exertion are within my range of direct perception;
however, dharma and adharma are not within my range of direct perception.
Among these qualities, how many are produced and how many are unproduced?
The entities of sensation, pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, diligence, vigor, the dharma, the non-dharma, conduct, detachment from those, this entity, and sound are exclusively produced;
the remainder are either produced or not produced.
If color, taste, fragrance, and tangibility belong to earth, they are all produced.
However, the combination of atoms of liquid moisture—consisting of color, taste, and tangibility—is not produced.
The combination of dyads and their effects is produced.
The substantial entity (*dravya*) is likewise: as that which is not produced is eternal, so too is that which is produced [regarding its] permanence or impermanence.
As it is with water, so it is with fire, with color and touch, and with the touch of wind.
All liquids within the earth and fire are produced.

First, in terms of number, and second, in terms of distinct entities, they follow the nature of being produced or unproduced; through the real aggregation of the produced and the unproduced, they constitute that which is both produced and unproduced.
The two types of substantiality (*dravya*), the two types of number (*saṃkhyā*), and the two types of distinct substantiality (*pṛthaktva*)—all are produced (*kṛtaka*).
Greatness (*mahattva*), minuteness (*aṇutva*), shortness (*hrasvatva*), and length (*dīrghatva*)—all are produced.
Sphericity (*parimaṇḍalatva*) is entirely unproduced (*akṛtaka*).
All that is resistant and all that is both resistant and non-resistant are produced.
As it is with the produced and the unproduced, so it is with the permanent and the impermanent.
Among these qualities, sound, touch, color-form, taste, and odor are each apprehended by a single faculty.
Number, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, that-ness, this-ness, fluidity, moisture, and momentum are perceived by the tactile sense-organ (*kāyendriya*).
Among these qualities (*guṇa*), which serve as the cause for which?
Regarding color, taste, odor, and touch, those that have homogeneous [qualities] as their cause refer to the aggregation of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and other such effects.
Regarding those for which fire is the cooperating cause: these are the atoms of color, taste, odor, and tangibility belonging to earth;
the liquid substances belonging to earth and fire; and the heavy substances belonging to earth and water.
Furthermore, all liquid substances of water, such as the two atoms (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, have their own homogeneous class as the cause for their aggregation.
Similarly, the single number and the distinct individuality of the two atoms and so forth have their own homogeneous class as the cause for their aggregation.
Two substances and so forth, as well as two distinct substances and so forth—whether of the same class or different classes—serve as causes.
A single substance and distinct substances serve as the cause for that cognition.
A large substance and a long substance have multiple substances as their cause.
The gross body and the long body take the accumulation of [atoms] as their cause.
The subtle body and the short body take both types of bodies as their cause.
Conjunction and disjunction take either individual action or simultaneous action and conjunction/disjunction as their cause.
The cognition of that entity and this entity as being identical, simultaneous, related, or dependent on distance and proximity serves as the cause.
Wisdom is of two kinds: namely, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

Direct perception is of four kinds: first, cognition of doubt; second, cognition of definitive certainty; third, erroneous cognition; and fourth, correct cognition. What serves as the cause for the cognition of doubt?

It is not the case that a single cognition of a common property (*sāmānyadharma*), preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and depending on the conjunction of various distinct mental states (*smṛti*) and the self (*ātman*),
serves as the cause for what kind of cognition is called "doubtful cognition" (*saṃśayajñāna*). What,
then, is the cause of "definitive cognition" (*niścayajñāna*)?
Doubtful cognition (vicikitsā-jñāna) takes as its cause the synthesis of my own mental states, preceded by hesitation and awaiting various distinct signs.
That which is certain is called definitive cognition (niścaya-jñāna).
What serves as the cause for false cognition (mithyā-jñāna)?

It is not the case that a single uniform dharma, preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), serves as the cause for a definitive cognition (*niścaya-jñāna*) that depends upon various distinct views and the conjunction of the self and the mental faculty;
such a definitive cognition is called false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
What, then, is the cause of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?

It is not the case that non-erroneous cognition—known as right knowledge—is preceded by a single commonality perceived through direct perception, nor does it depend on the causal conjunction of a distinct direct perception of each [object] with the self and the mind.
This non-erroneous cognition is called right knowledge.

As it is with direct perception, so it is with inference. There are three kinds of direct perception: first, that produced by the conjunction of four; second, that produced by the conjunction of three; and third, that produced by the conjunction of two. Regarding the conjunction of four: [it is] produced by the conjunction of the four elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and the consciousness that arises from them. Regarding the conjunction of three: [it is] produced by the conjunction of three elements and the consciousness that arises from them. Regarding the conjunction of two: [it is] produced by the conjunction of two elements and the consciousness that arises from them. Furthermore, there is that produced by the conjunction of the sense organ, the object, and consciousness. This is called the threefold conjunction. As for the conjunction of four, it refers to the conjunction of the sense organ, the object, consciousness, and mental factors (*caitta*). This is called the fourfold conjunction. Thus, these are the three types of direct perception. As for inference, it is of two kinds: inference based on what has been seen and inference based on what has been heard. Inference based on what has been seen is of two types: inference through similarity and inference through dissimilarity. Inference based on what has been heard is likewise of two types: inference through similarity and inference through dissimilarity. These are the two types of inference. Therefore, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the effect, inference of the cause, and inference of the nature of things. Inference of the effect is, for example, inferring rain from the swelling of a river. Inference of the cause is, for example, inferring a past fire from seeing smoke. Inference of the nature of things is, for example, inferring that sound is impermanent because it is produced. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the past, inference of the future, and inference of the present. Inference of the past is, for example, inferring that one previously experienced a certain object. Inference of the future is, for example, inferring that one will experience a certain object later. Inference of the present is, for example, inferring that a certain object currently exists. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: internal inference, external inference, and both internal and external inference. Internal inference is, for example, inferring one's own mind. External inference is, for example, inferring another's mind. Both internal and external inference is, for example, inferring the existence of a self. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference for oneself, inference for others, and inference for both oneself and others. Inference for oneself is, for example, when one understands a meaning through reasoning alone. Inference for others is, for example, when one explains a meaning through logical arguments. Inference for both oneself and others is, for example, when one both understands and explains a meaning. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference based on scripture, inference based on logic, and inference based on both scripture and logic. Inference based on scripture is, for example, accepting the teachings of the Buddha as authoritative. Inference based on logic is, for example, establishing a conclusion through correct reasoning. Inference based on both scripture and logic is, for example, accepting the Buddha’s teachings while also verifying them through rational analysis. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: weak inference, medium inference, and strong inference. Weak inference is, for example, when the evidence is insufficient or the reasoning is fallacious. Medium inference is, for example, when the evidence is somewhat sufficient but lacks full certainty. Strong inference is, for example, when the evidence is conclusive and the reasoning is unassailable. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference concerning the conventional, inference concerning the ultimate, and inference concerning both the conventional and the ultimate. Inference concerning the conventional is, for example, inferring the various phenomena of the world. Inference concerning the ultimate is, for example, inferring the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Inference concerning both the conventional and the ultimate is, for example, inferring the relationship between phenomena and their ultimate nature. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the known, inference of the unknown, and inference of the partially known. Inference of the known is, for example, when one has already experienced an object and now infers its recurrence. Inference of the unknown is, for example, when one infers an object never before experienced. Inference of the partially known is, for example, when one infers an object based on partial characteristics. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the manifest, inference of the hidden, and inference of the obscure. Inference of the manifest is, for example, inferring a visible object. Inference of the hidden is, for example, inferring an invisible object. Inference of the obscure is, for example, inferring an object that is difficult to discern. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the primary, inference of the secondary, and inference of the derivative. Inference of the primary is, for example, inferring the fundamental cause. Inference of the secondary is, for example, inferring the resulting effects. Inference of the derivative is, for example, inferring the specific variations of those effects. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the self, inference of the other, and inference of the non-self. Inference of the self is, for example, inferring the nature of one's own continuum. Inference of the other is, for example, inferring the nature of another's continuum. Inference of the non-self is, for example, inferring the nature of all phenomena as being devoid of a self. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the wholesome, inference of the unwholesome, and inference of the neutral. Inference of the wholesome is, for example, inferring the path to liberation. Inference of the unwholesome is, for example, inferring the causes of suffering. Inference of the neutral is, for example, inferring the nature of conditioned phenomena as being neither inherently wholesome nor unwholesome. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the past, inference of the future, and inference of the present. Inference of the past is, for example, inferring the karmic seeds of former lives. Inference of the future is, for example, inferring the results of future karma. Inference of the present is, for example, inferring the conditions of the current moment. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the internal, inference of the external, and inference of the internal-external. Inference of the internal is, for example, inferring the state of one's own mind. Inference of the external is, for example, inferring the state of the external world. Inference of the internal-external is, for example, inferring the interaction between the internal and external. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the coarse, inference of the subtle, and inference of the extremely subtle. Inference of the coarse is, for example, inferring gross material objects. Inference of the subtle is, for example, inferring the subtle elements. Inference of the extremely subtle is, for example, inferring the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*). These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the worldly, inference of the supramundane, and inference of the mundane-supramundane. Inference of the worldly is, for example, inferring the phenomena of saṃsāra. Inference of the supramundane is, for example, inferring the phenomena of nirvāṇa. Inference of the mundane-supramundane is, for example, inferring the phenomena of the bodhisattva path. These are the three types of inference. Thus, direct perception and inference are each of three kinds. Furthermore, inference is also of three kinds: inference of the dharma, inference of the person, and inference of the dharma-person. What is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

It is the cognition of characteristics regarding that which is present: color, taste, odor, tangible objects, number, individuality, conjunction, disjunction, "that-ness," "this-ness," heaviness, fluidity, moisture, and functional capacity.
Earth, water, fire, and solidity possess the nature of having grasping and so forth as their activity;
with the exception of sound, the composite possesses both capacity and incapacity, which constitutes the nature of sound.
Regarding the common portion, there is the cognition of both capacity and incapacity.
The fourfold conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and the mind serves as the cause;
from this threefold conjunction, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises. What is this direct perception?

That is to say, regarding sound and the capacity or incapacity within the conjunction of sound, as well as the cognition of the nature and existence of the object, there is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) produced by the conjunction of the three—self, sense faculty, and mind.
How is it that this arises from the conjunction of two?

It refers to the cognition regarding the objects of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, as well as the objects of their respective capacities and incapacities, and the nature of existence and non-existence;
this [cognition] arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind.
Inference based on cause (*kāraṇānumāna*) refers to that which is preceded by a cognition of the conjunction of a single object and its contradictory [disjunction];
it depends upon the recollection of relations such as conjunction, taking the conjunction of the self and the mind as its cause.
Pleasure and pain depend on the combination of the four factors—dharma, adharma, past actions, and the conjunction [of the elements]—as their cause.
Desire and aversion depend on the combination of pleasure and pain, attention, false knowledge, and the mental faculty (*manas*) as their cause.
Effort depends on the combination of desire, aversion, and the mental faculty as its cause, as well as the life-force (*jīvitendriya*) as its condition.
Because of non-desire, it serves as the cause for the activity of inhalation and exhalation.
What serves as the cause for the activity of momentum? It takes as its cause the momentum produced by the activity of gathering and hurling.

With desire for the dharma or non-dharma and hatred as the precursor, and depending upon hearing and mindfulness, one distances oneself from what is non-dharmic; taking the union of the self and the mind together with the subtle process capable of accomplishing the pure or the impure as its cause.
Regarding the consideration of causes, the operation of perceptual, inferential, and scriptural knowledge, combined with the activity of my own intention, constitutes the cause.
Sound is of three kinds: first, that produced by conjunction; second, that produced by disjunction; and third, that produced by sound itself.
As for that produced by conjunction, it has as its cause the contact of tangible substances, the presence of their functional efficacy, and the conjunction of tangible substances with empty space.

Regarding the production of sound through separation: there is a real contact possessing the potential for separation, and this real contact, together with the potential for separation, takes the empty space as its cause.
Regarding the production of sound through conjunction: there is a real contact possessing the potential for conjunction and separation, and this takes the unobstructed empty space as its cause.
Among these twenty-four qualities, how many depend on a single reality, and how many depend on that which is not a single reality?
They are: color, taste, fragrance, tangibility, dimension, that substance, this substance, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, effort, virtue, non-virtue, action, and heaviness of substance.
Fluidity, moisture, momentum, and sound—these twenty-one [characteristics] all depend on a single real entity (*dravya*).
Conjunction and disjunction depend on two real entities.
Number depends either on a single real entity or on multiple real entities.
What is it that depends on a single reality? It is the number one.
What is it that depends on non-single realities? It is the numbers two, three, and so forth.
As it is with numbers, so it is with distinct entities.
Among these twenty-four qualities, how many are pervasive bases and how many are non-pervasive bases?
Color, taste, odor, touch, number, distinctness, individuality, that-ness, this-ness, fluidity, moisture, heaviness, and momentum are pervasive bases.
The others do not pervade their substrata.
Among these twenty-four qualities, which are mutually contradictory?
Sound produced by conjunction and disjunction is contradictory to all other sounds, which are its effects, as well as to the primary elements that produce them.
The fruit of the Dharma, joy, and right knowledge is contrary [to their opposites].
The fruit of non-Dharma, suffering, and false knowledge is contrary [to their opposites].
The fruit of all-knowledge and conduct is contrary [to their opposites].
Discriminative knowledge contradicts the fruit of all-knowing conduct;
the final sound contradicts all causes.
Finally, my virtue is also like this:
pleasure and pain are contrary in their results,
while dharma and adharma are contrary in their causes.
Desire, hatred, and exertion have effects that are mutually contradictory;
pleasure and pain have causes that are mutually contradictory;
and the same applies to all intermediate sounds.
The self, virtue, effort, suffering, contact, and existence—these two [sets] are not contradictory as cause and effect.
Volitional formations, the self, virtue, conduct, mindfulness, and causes are not contradictory as cause and effect with suffering.
The practice of mindfulness contradicts its cause;
the causal act of contact is a real conjunction that does not contradict its effect;
and the number "two" and so forth do not contradict their effect, which is dual cognition.
Just as with two entities and so forth, where the number "two" refers to distinct entities, it is the same for that entity and this entity.
Regarding the atoms of earth that exist as a combination of form, taste, odor, and touch, their conjunction with the great [elements] does not contradict the relationship of cause and effect.
The alternating states of conjunction and separation are not cause and effect, as they are mutually contradictory.

However, the real, ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) of form and so forth, which act as the primary producers (*bhūta*), do not contradict their homogeneous effects, such as the two-atom clusters (*dvyaṇuka*) and other similar forms, which are of the same class.
Finally, the substantial matter (dravya-rūpa) of the final moment of the continuum and its subsequent fruits are of the same class as their causal matter and do not contradict it;
likewise, all the intervening substantial matter of the continuum and its homogeneous fruits do not contradict their causal matter.
The single substance (dravya) and [the qualities] such as color (rūpa) are not mutually contradictory as cause and effect.
All qualities (guṇa) are not contradictory with substance.
Thus, among these twenty-four qualities, how many possess substance and how many lack substance?
All that exists is real.
Just as that which is real is devoid of qualities, devoid of activity, and is not a cause of aggregation— these being the marks of a reality possessing qualities—
the same applies to that which is non-obstructive and without parts.
Regarding these five types of karma, how many are substantial and how many are non-substantial?
All of them are substantial.

As with that which is substantial, they rely upon a single reality that is without material obstruction, without qualities, without fineness, and without separation or conjunction; they function as causes and effects, yet they do not constitute the signs of an accumulated reality.
The causes upon which actions such as gathering and throwing depend are likewise not of the same kind [as their effects].
Thus, regarding these five types of karma, what do they rely upon and in what substance?
The action of grasping relies upon all [four] elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—as well as the mind.
The same applies to the karma of grasping, the karma of relinquishing, and the karma of movement.
As for the karma of contraction, it relies upon a result that is extremely relaxed, subtle, and arranged with distinctions, being large, long, and solid.
As it is with the action of contracting, so it is with the action of extending.
Among these five types of action, how many have a pervasive basis and how many have a non-pervasive basis?
All of them have a pervasive basis.
Some say that karma which depends on a single atom is a pervasive basis,
whereas that which depends on two atoms or more is a non-pervasive basis.
Such being the case, if these various karmas are internal...
With the body and its causal conditions, the nose, tongue, skin, eye-faculties, and mind are combined as the causes and conditions for conjunction.
Among these, bodily action is primary; it is preceded by desire, and through my application of effort, it serves as the cause and condition for non-conjunction.
The second category likewise takes action as the cause and condition for non-conjunction.
This applies to bodily actions, mental actions, and subtle actions as well.

Regarding the initial [category] of olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and visual actions, the conjunction of the self with effort and the conjunction of the body serve as the cause and condition for non-conjunction.
The second category likewise takes action as the cause and condition for non-conjunction;
this is the case with the actions of the nose and so forth in relation to implements such as pestles, as well as the actions of the body in relation to garlands, necklaces, ointments, and perfumes.
Regarding "the body of one who sleeps falls":
for the first [case], heaviness serves as the cause and condition for non-conjunction;
for the second and subsequent [cases], the action of the heavy substance serves as the cause and condition for non-conjunction.
Whether one who is asleep performs the activity of inhalation and exhalation or not depends on their intention;
therefore, in the first case, the causal conditions consist of the primary life-faculty, preceded by exertion, and the conjunction of the self with the body as the cause of non-disjunction.
The second and subsequent [factors] likewise take action as the cause of non-conjunction.
Just as the first instance of flowing water takes liquidity as the cause of non-conjunction,
the second and subsequent instances take the action of liquidity as the cause of non-conjunction.
Regarding the first [case], where fire burns above and wind fans from the side:
it is because the factors of dharma and non-dharma, conjoined with a self, constitute the causes and conditions for non-conjunction.
The second and subsequent cases are as previously explained.
The primary karma that serves as the causal condition for the formation of the body consists of the four great elements and the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Furthermore, through the conjunction of phenomena (*dharma*), non-phenomena (*adharma*), and the self (*ātman*), there arises the causal condition of non-conjunction.
The second [category] and so forth are as previously explained.
The same applies to the karma that causes the formation of a body, the transformation of trees and so forth, and the conjunction of two atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Regarding the initial karma of mental orientation and aversion:
it takes dharma and adharma together as the causal conditions for conjunction and non-conjunction.
The second [point] and so forth are as previously explained.
Regarding the first [point], the maturation of the benefit or non-benefit of sentient beings through the karma of the stages and bases:
it is because the self, by means of dharma and non-dharma, acts as the causal condition for conjunction and non-conjunction.
The second [category] is as previously explained.

Regarding the karma associated with throwing or striking upon earth, water, or fire, it takes the heavy nature of solids and the fluidity of liquids, along with the force of vigorous effort, as the causal conditions for their non-conjunction.
According to what is appropriate, there are actions such as grasping:
if it occurs in fire, the heavy substance is removed; if in wind, the liquid substance is removed; if in the mind, striking and hurling are removed.
Thus, does this nature exist as something produced or as something unproduced?
That which is unproduced (*akṛtaka*) is certainly [permanent].
Just as that which is unproduced is permanent, so too is it devoid of qualities (*guṇa*), devoid of activity (*kriyā*), devoid of parts (*avayava*), and likewise [devoid of these].

There exist real qualities, actions, and commonalities; there is the capacity and incapacity to exclude [others], the distinction between the shared and the specific, the combined, the unified, and the commonality of designations, conditions, and causes.

There exists another, distinct from the actual transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which is a single reality that excludes other causes for cognition; it indicates that this cause for cognition is empty, and it functions throughout space and time.
This cause for the conceptualization of space and so forth is eternal, unconditioned, devoid of qualities, devoid of activity, and without parts.
Excluding that which possesses existence, and the various distinct portions of both the capable and the incapable, the composite is not manifold.
This composite is a single unity, eternal, unconditioned, partless, and non-obstructive.

All real entities—whether qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*karman*), whether characterized by identity or difference, whether capable or incapable, and those belonging to both categories—arise from causes and conditions that are common to them; they are expressed by the same designations and share the same objective referents (*ālambana*).
Thus, that which is capable is the object of action (*kriyā*), while that which is not capable is not the object of action.
That which is unproduced (*akṛtaka*) is necessarily eternal;
as it is unproduced, so too is it devoid of qualities (*guṇa*), devoid of activity (*kriyā*), devoid of parts (*avayava*), and devoid of resistance (*sapratigha*).

Regarding substance (*dravya*), quality, and action, each is distinct [from the others] in terms of their specific exclusion (*apoha*), their commonality, their capacity or incapacity, their shared and unique portions, their difference, their conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and their non-identity as the referents of linguistic expressions and the objects of cognition.
This is what is meant by "capacity" and "incapacity" being likewise so.
It is the single unity integrated with the meaning of the pervasive category of real nature (tattva),
which is non-obstructive, partless, inactive, devoid of qualities, eternal, and uncreated.
The various substances (dravya), though mutually related, are distinct from this [substance] itself as well as from qualities (guṇa) and actions (karma).
The same applies to their respective natures: the nature of quality, the nature of action, and the nature of substance.
Among these five kinds of non-designatable categories (avaktavyapada-artha), how many are eternal (nitya) and how many are impermanent (anitya)?
The non-existence of that which has not yet arisen is impermanent because it is contradictory to the arising of real qualities and activities;
whereas the non-existence of that which has already ceased, mutual non-existence, and absolute non-existence are all permanent because they do not contradict reality and so forth.
It is not the case that the non-existent is eternal or that the eternal is impermanent.
How so? Just as the earth and other [elements] are real, yet their other qualities do not combine [with them];
likewise, if reality (*tattva*), etc., were identical or different, or possessed capacity or lack thereof, they would not combine with anything other than their own substratum.
If there were an inherent nature that does not harmonize with its own kind, how could impermanence be real?
For although two realities may not yet be conjoined, they will necessarily become so; thus, [the former] would not exist in relation to the latter.
If that which exists in reality possesses real qualities and activities, they must necessarily be conjoined; yet such [qualities and activities] do not exist in this [subject].
Regarding these five types of non-existence (*abhāva*), how many are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and how many are not objects of direct perception?
All things that are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and do not depend on others for their occurrence are objects of inference (*anumāna*).
Among these ten categories of meaning, how many are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and how many are not?
All of them are objects of knowledge; they are precisely these.
*Vyākhyāna-hetu-viśeṣa-siddhānta-daśapadārtha-śāstra*, one fascicle.
